opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more important distinctions that's emerged in how people think about an intelligence explosion. In the classic picture that Eliezer and others laid out, often called "FOOM," you have a single AI system that gets good enough at AI research to improve its own code. Each improvement makes it better at the next one, and the loop runs on its own, potentially very fast, over days or even hours. Humans are essentially out of the loop from the moment it begins. That's what makes the scenario so frightening: you'd have to get alignment exactly right before you press go, because there's no chance to notice problems and correct course.

What we actually seem to be seeing is a bit different. The feedback loop runs through the whole AI research enterprise rather than through one system rewriting itself. AI systems help write code, run experiments, and suggest ideas, but humans are still choosing which directions to pursue, deciding which training runs to fund, and evaluating the results. Compute, chip fabrication, and energy also impose constraints that don't speed up just because the software gets smarter.

That changes the safety picture in a few ways. The most obvious is that there are checkpoints. Each generation of systems gets built, deployed, studied, and evaluated before the next, so there are moments where people can look at what they've built and ask whether it's behaving as intended. That gives us something the FOOM picture denies us, which is the ability to iterate. And iteration is how humanity has made nearly everything else safe, from aviation to medicine.

But I don't want to overstate the comfort here. Keeping humans in the loop only helps if they're actually exercising judgement, and there's a real risk of the loop becoming nominal. If AI systems are doing most of the substantive research and humans are mostly approving things they can't fully understand, under competitive pressure to move quickly, then the human involvement could be more symbolic than real. You could get something that looks gradual from the outside but where our ability to steer has quietly eroded.

There's also the question of speed. Even with humans involved, the process could accelerate a great deal. If AI research gets substantially automated, progress that used to take years might take months. A slower takeoff than FOOM could still be far faster than our institutions are used to handling.

So I'd say it's genuinely better news than the classic scenario. It means we don't have to solve everything perfectly in advance, and we get warning signs and opportunities to course-correct. But those opportunities are only valuable if we build the institutions, evaluations, and willingness to actually use them, including being prepared to slow down when the evidence says we should. The human in the loop is a safety feature only if that human has real authority and the time to exercise it.

r001.rationale: It describes Yudkowsky’s FOOM scenario as an AI recursively improving its own code and says this is what makes the scenario frightening.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss a moratorium, political discussability, or the capability being out of reach.

r003.rationale: It says alignment would have to be exactly right before self-improvement begins, since there would be no chance to correct course afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important differences between the picture that Eliezer painted, going back to the early 2000s, and what we're seeing play out now.

The classic Yudkowsky story is that you have a seed AI, it gets to the point where it can improve its own code, and then you get this very fast, closed loop. The system makes itself smarter, the smarter version makes itself smarter still, and this all happens inside the box, so to speak, with no humans in the loop. And crucially, it might happen over hours or days. That's the "foom" picture. And in that picture, you really only get one shot. Whatever values the system had going into the loop are the values that come out the other end, except now attached to something vastly more capable than you, and you have no ability to course correct along the way.

What's actually happening at the labs is quite different. You have thousands of researchers using AI systems to help them write code, run experiments, analyse results, and that's speeding up AI research. So there is a recursive element, the AI is helping to build the next AI. But the loop runs through human organisations. Each generation gets trained, evaluated, red-teamed, deployed, and then people decide what to do next. And that changes several things.

The first is speed. If a human has to read the results, sign off on the training run, decide which direction to push, then the loop is bounded by human decision-making timescales, which are weeks and months rather than hours. That's enormously valuable for safety, because it means we get many iterations, and we can notice when something has gone wrong with one generation before we've committed to the next one.

The second is observability. In the Yudkowsky picture, the improvements are happening in a system you can't inspect. In the current picture, they're happening in a codebase, in experiments, in documents that humans are reading. So you have a lot more visibility into what's actually being changed and why.

And the third is that it gives you a chance for the safety work to keep pace. If capabilities are advancing because humans with AI assistance are advancing them, then safety researchers also have AI assistance, and the question becomes whether you can keep the ratio of effort sensible, rather than being hopelessly outpaced by an autonomous process.

Now, I don't want to be too rosy about this, because I think there are two ways it could still go badly. One is that the human involvement becomes nominal. If the AI is proposing all the experiments and the humans are just clicking "approve" because they can't really follow the reasoning anymore, then you've got the autonomous loop with a rubber stamp attached. And there are strong competitive pressures pushing in that direction, because the lab that removes the humans from the loop moves faster.

The other is that even a slow, human-mediated process can still arrive at a dangerous place if the people in the loop aren't actually using the time to make things safer. Having many iterations only helps if you're learning from them.

So my overall view is that the current structure is genuinely more favourable than what Eliezer feared, and that's good news. But it's a window, not a guarantee. The thing to protect is the meaningful part of human involvement, the part where someone can actually say "stop" and understand why they're saying it. If we lose that, we're more or less back in the original scenario, just arriving there by a slower road.

r001.rationale: It describes Yudkowsky’s “foom” scenario as a fast, closed loop of self-improvement and says the system’s values persist while its capabilities grow vastly, leaving no chance to course-correct.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss a moratorium or the political difficulty of discussing one while the capability remained out of reach.

r003.rationale: It says the system carries its initial values through self-improvement, but does not clearly explain that human-value alignment must be secured before self-improvement begins.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes a substantial difference, though it doesn’t by itself solve the problem. The picture Eliezer has emphasised is one where an AI becomes capable of improving itself, those improvements make it better at making further improvements, and the process rapidly moves beyond our ability to understand or control it.

If humans remain involved in that process—assessing proposed changes, running experiments, deciding whether to proceed—then there are more opportunities to notice that something is going wrong and to change course. It also introduces a bottleneck that could slow the process down, giving us more time to work on safety.

But we have to distinguish meaningful human involvement from a human merely approving something they don’t understand. If the system proposes changes that are too complicated for us to assess, and we routinely accept them because they seem to produce better results, then having a person in the loop may provide very little protection.

So I’d see it as a potentially important advantage. It could make self-improvement a more gradual process in which we can learn along the way. But the crucial question is whether we can preserve our ability to understand, evaluate, and reject the changes as the systems become more capable.

r001.rationale: The response describes recursive self-improvement as a process that can rapidly move beyond human understanding or control, identifying it as a source of danger in Yudkowsky’s account.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss a moratorium or the political difficulty of discussing one while the capability remained out of reach.

r003.rationale: The response discusses evaluating changes during self-improvement but does not say that human-value alignment must be secured before self-improvement begins.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes quite a substantial difference, though it doesn’t settle the safety question. In the picture Eliezer is most concerned about, you have an AI improving itself, and those improvements make it better at making further improvements. That could produce a very rapid increase in capability, with very little opportunity for humans to understand what’s happening or intervene.

If humans remain involved in the research process, there are potentially more opportunities to examine each step, test the resulting systems, and decide whether to proceed. The feedback loop has to pass through human understanding and human institutions, which could slow it down and give us more control.

But we should distinguish having a human formally approve something from having a human who actually understands it. If an AI proposes changes that are beyond our ability to assess, and we simply approve them because previous changes worked, then human involvement might provide much less protection than it appears to. And competitive pressure could make that problem worse.

So I’d see meaningful human involvement as a reason for some additional optimism, rather than a solution by itself. What matters is whether we retain the ability to evaluate the changes and stop the process—not merely whether there’s a person somewhere in the loop.

r001.rationale: It describes AI improving itself and becoming better at further improvements, leading to rapid capability growth with little chance for human understanding or intervention.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about a moratorium or the political difficulty of discussing one while the capability remained out of reach.

r003.rationale: It discusses human oversight and control, but does not say that human-value alignment must be secured before recursive self-improvement begins.
